  8
 May 22, 2025

CalBay Development LLC
Attention: Ryan Shea
120 W. Lime Street
Monrovia, CA 91016

Via email: ryan@calbaycorp.com

Expiration of Conditional Use Permit (CUP) PL23-0032 –1,200 square foot “take out only”
building pad café with drive-through.

Address: 9501 Atlantic Avenue
Case #: PL23-0032

Dear Mr. Shea:

On March 5, 2024, the South Gate Planning Commission Issued you Conditional Use Permit
No. PL23-0032 (the “CUP”). The CUP allowed you, subject to conditions, to operate a 1,200
square foot “take out only” building pad café with drive-through located at 9501 Atlantic Avenue,
in the CDR 2 (Corridor 2) zone.

Although the CUP was issued by the Planning Commission, you did not operate the subject
property for the uses authorized by the CUP within the required timeframe. Pursuant to
Condition No. 13 of the CUP: “This approval is valid for a period of 12 months from the date of
final determination. If the use approved by this action is not established within such a period of
time, this approval shall terminate and shall be null and void.”

Accordingly, the CUP expired on March 5, 2025, and the CUP is now considered null and void.

If you wish to pursue this project further, you must initiate a new entitlement process by
submitting your application materials to planninginfo@sogate.org.

If you have any questions, please feel free to contact me at (323) 563-9514 or
jvaldez@sogate.org.

Sincerely,

Joshua Valdez
Associate Planner

  Core Purpose of The
  Brown Act
  “The people of this State do not yield their sovereignty to the agencies which serve
 them. The people, in delegating authority, do not give their public servants the right to
  decide what is good for the people to know and what is not good for them to know.
  The people insist on remaining informed so that they may retain control over the
  instruments they have created.” – Government Code § 54950

   TRANSPARENCY

  Why do we need the Ralph M. Brown Act?
   What does it seek to accomplish?
   How does it achieve its purpose?

  24
 HISTORY OF
THE BROWN ACT
 Authored by Ralph M. Brown (1908-1966), the Legislature adopted the
  Brown Act in 1953 to protect and promote the public's right to access and
  participation in local government meetings.
 “All meetings of the legislative body of a local agency shall be open and
  public, and all persons shall be permitted to attend any meeting of the
  legislative body, except as otherwise provided in this chapter."
 Legislative bodies covered by the Brown Act should conduct their affairs
  as openly and transparent as possible with few exceptions.
 The Brown Act is found at California Government Code Sections 54950-
  54963.

  5

MEETINGS:
WHEN DOES THE BROWN ACT APPLY?
Meetings Defined (by current statute):
 Congregation of a majority of the members of a
  legislative body
 To hear, discuss or deliberate City business
 Can include use of technology (email, phone, Zoom) by
  a majority of board members to discuss an issue
 Meeting requires quorum to get started and stay in
  business  6
  25
 MEETINGS:
WHEN DOES THE BROWN ACT NOT APPLY?
 Individual contacts & conversations
 Conferences open to the public (e.g., annual association conferences)
 Open and publicized community meetings (e.g., local service club)
 Other legislative bodies (e.g., members of city council attending meeting
  of planning commission)
 Social/ceremonial events (e.g. football game, wedding, retirement party,
  etc.)

  WHAT ARE DISRUPTIVE COMMENTS?
 WHITE v. CITY OF NORWALK (9th Cir. 1990) 900 F. 2d 1421

 • “[A] City Council meeting is still just that, a governmental process
  with a governmental purpose. The Council has an agenda to be
  addressed and dealt with.

 • “A speaker may disrupt by speaking too long, by being unduly
  repetitious, or by extended discussion of irrelevancies. The meeting
  is disrupted because the Council is prevented from accomplishing
  its business in a reasonably efficient manner. Indeed, such conduct
  may interfere with the rights of other speakers.”
